ap_psychology-m21.stem: A meta-analysis combines the results of 25 studies of gratitude journaling and finds an average effect size of d = 0.15 on well-being. (Effect sizes of about 0.2 or less are called small, 0.3 to 0.7 medium, and 0.8 or more large.) Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: Gratitude journaling has a large effect on well-being, because combining many studies always increases the size of an effect.
options.why: Combining studies estimates the average effect; it does not increase its size, and 0.15 is small.

options.text: The effect is not meaningful at all, because any effect size below 0.2 is treated as exactly zero by researchers.
options.why: Effect sizes of about 0.2 or less are described as small, not as zero.

options.text: Across many studies, gratitude journaling has a small effect on well-being on average.
options.why: A meta-analysis combines results from many studies, and an effect size of 0.15 is in the range usually called small.

options.text: The meta-analysis is one large experiment with 25 conditions, so by itself it shows that gratitude journaling causes better well-being.
options.why: A meta-analysis combines separate studies and its causal strength depends on the designs of those studies.

ap_psychology-m22.stem: A researcher wants to learn how members of a large student club describe their sense of belonging, so she asks the same set of questions of 400 members. Which design is being used, and what is a main limitation?

options.text: Survey; responses may be affected by self-report problems such as social desirability bias.
options.why: A survey collects self-reports from many people with the same questions, and respondents may answer in ways that make them look good.

options.text: Naturalistic observation; the researcher cannot control the behavior of club members while recording what they do.
options.why: The researcher is asking questions, not observing behavior without interference.

options.text: Experiment; the researcher did not randomly assign members to different versions of the club before asking the questions.
options.why: No variable is manipulated, so this is not an experiment.

options.text: Case study; the findings from a single club member cannot be generalized to a group of 400 members.
options.why: The researcher asked 400 members, not one member in depth.

ap_psychology-m22.stem: A researcher wants to record how often drivers yield to pedestrians at a crosswalk without influencing anyone's behavior. Which design is most appropriate, and what is its main limitation?

options.text: Experiment; the researcher cannot choose which drivers approach the crosswalk, so random assignment is impossible.
options.why: The goal is to observe existing behavior, and an experiment would require manipulating conditions that could change it.

options.text: Survey; drivers may report what seems socially desirable instead of what they actually did at the crosswalk.
options.why: A survey would measure self-reports rather than behavior, so it does not meet the goal of recording actual behavior unobtrusively.

options.text: Naturalistic observation; it cannot show why drivers behave the way they do.
options.why: Naturalistic observation records behavior as it occurs without interference, but it does not control variables or explain causes.

options.text: Case study; the findings from one driver may not describe how other drivers behave at the crosswalk.
options.why: A case study examines one person in depth, which does not fit the goal of recording how often many drivers yield.
